quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: Hydrogen trains are being tested as a replacement for diesel on railway lines that are too quiet to justify the expense of electrification. Their fuel cells combine hydrogen with oxygen to produce electricity, emitting only water vapour. In a two-year trial in northern Germany, the trains ran reliably, carried passengers at speeds comparable to diesel units and needed refuelling only once a day. However, the picture is less green than it appears. Most hydrogen today is made from natural gas, which releases carbon, and cleaner production using renewable electricity is still costly. Operators also need special fuelling stations, and a few regions that ordered trains have since switched to battery models, which have proved cheaper on short routes. Supporters accept these points but say hydrogen may suit longer lines where batteries cannot carry enough energy. Rail companies in the UK and Japan are running similar tests, and engineers say that the technology is easier to introduce on lines where no cables have been installed. A typical hydrogen train costs about a third more than a diesel one to buy. Trials in other regions have used hydrogen produced from surplus wind power, which cuts emissions but adds to the price.
quests.question: How does the passage assess hydrogen trains overall?
options: Hydrogen trains work but their environmental and cost benefits are limited so far
Battery trains are always superior to hydrogen on every kind of route
Diesel trains are cleaner than they appear and should be kept for now
Hydrogen trains have failed completely and are being withdrawn from service
quests.correctAnswer: Hydrogen trains work but their environmental and cost benefits are limited so far
quests.hint: Weigh the trial's positive results against the complications after "However".
quests.explanation: The trial succeeded technically, but the fuel's origin, costs and competition from batteries qualify the benefits. The passage neither rejects nor fully endorses the technology.

quests.instruction: Read the passage efficiently, then answer the question.
quests.passage: A village that lost its bus service five years ago now has a mobile library that stops at three points each week. The van carries about two thousand books, a few computers and, more importantly, a librarian who knows most borrowers by name. Loans are highest among older residents and families with young children, groups that find it hardest to travel to the town library. The librarian often helps people with tasks that have little to do with books, such as filling in online forms or printing tickets. The library began as an experiment funded by a lottery grant, and the number of loans has grown every year since. Volunteers help to carry heavy boxes and to read to children during the summer holidays. The regular stops include a care home, a village hall and the car park outside the primary school. The county council, which is under pressure to save money, has proposed replacing the van with a home-delivery scheme. Users have objected, arguing that the visit itself matters: it is where neighbours meet, and the printed page is only part of what the van provides.
quests.question: What do users mean when they say the visit "itself matters"?
options: The council pays for their travel tickets
Delivery is faster than waiting for a visit
The social contact is as important as the borrowed books
The van is more valuable than the books it carries
quests.correctAnswer: The social contact is as important as the borrowed books
quests.hint: Note what the users say the van provides beyond books.
quests.explanation: They value meeting neighbours and receiving help, which delivery would not provide. Books alone are not the reason for the visit.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: Job sharing, in which two people split one full-time role, has been available for decades but is still uncommon. Employers often worry about handovers and duplicated meetings, and many managers assume that a job's responsibilities cannot be divided. Yet evidence from organisations that have tried it is encouraging. In a hospital department that introduced shared management posts, patient satisfaction remained steady, and staff turnover in the department fell. The two people involved typically overlap for a day or half a day each week to exchange information, and many describe their partner as a source of support and a check on their own decisions. Part-time work of this kind is more popular among parents and carers, and a few managers who once doubted it now say they would recruit in the same way again. One difficulty is that partners must agree on how to handle disagreements. Recruiters report that applications for shared posts have grown steadily, particularly from people returning to work after a career break. The arrangement suits people who need flexibility, but its benefits reach wider: employers gain two sets of skills for the price of one salary, though they must pay for extra training and benefits.
quests.question: Which cost do employers face when using job sharing?
options: Extra training and benefits for two people
Two full salaries for the same job every month
Loss of patient satisfaction in the department
Higher staff turnover than before the change
quests.correctAnswer: Extra training and benefits for two people
quests.hint: The employers' extra costs are mentioned at the very end.
quests.explanation: Employers pay one salary between two people but must fund additional training and benefits. Turnover and satisfaction were not harmed.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: A new law would require social media platforms to verify users' ages and to block children under sixteen. Supporters say that early exposure to harmful content and constant comparison with others damage young people's mental health, and point to rising levels of anxiety. Critics agree that risks exist, but doubt that the law will work. Age checks depend on identity documents or facial scanning, both of which raise privacy concerns, and determined teenagers can use false details or borrow an adult's account. Australia has passed a similar law, and early reports suggest that thousands of accounts have been closed, though some young people have simply moved to smaller apps that are not covered by the rules. Parents' groups are divided about whether the law goes far enough. Some technology companies have said they would prefer national rules to a patchwork of local ones, which would be easier to follow. There is also the question of what would be lost: for isolated teenagers, online communities can be a lifeline. Some experts suggest that a better approach would be to require platforms to change how they operate, for example by turning off endless scrolling for young users, rather than simply excluding them.
quests.question: What alternative do some experts propose?
options: Allowing only adults to create accounts on any platform
Checking every user's identity documents at each login
Banning all social media for users under eighteen
Requiring platforms to change features rather than excluding young users
quests.correctAnswer: Requiring platforms to change features rather than excluding young users
quests.hint: The alternative is introduced by "better approach".
quests.explanation: These experts favour changes such as switching off endless scrolling. They do not endorse simply keeping teenagers out.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: In some care homes, small robots now keep residents company. One model, shaped like a seal, responds to touch with movements and gentle sounds. Studies suggest that residents with dementia become calmer and more talkative when interacting with it, and staff report fewer episodes of distress. Some have argued that a robot's warmth is an illusion, but the residents who respond to it do not seem to mind. Several families say they are pleased to see their relatives smiling during a visit for the first time in months. The seal costs several thousand dollars, so homes usually buy only a few and rotate them among the residents who benefit most. Yet many people find the idea uncomfortable. Ethicists ask whether it is right to give lonely people an imitation of companionship rather than real contact, and worry that the presence of the robots may allow families to visit less often. Care workers, in contrast, tend to be pragmatic: if a device reduces distress, it frees them to spend time on tasks that require human skills. The managers of one home say that they use the robots only as a supplement, and that human visits are never replaced.
quests.question: How do care workers generally regard the robots?
options: Practically, as a way to reduce distress and free their time
With deep suspicion, as a danger to their patients
As a replacement for family visits and staff time
As a threat to their jobs on the ward
quests.correctAnswer: Practically, as a way to reduce distress and free their time
quests.hint: Find the sentence introduced by "in contrast".
quests.explanation: Care workers focus on results: less distress and more time for tasks that require human skills. Ethicists raise the moral worries.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: When a phone screen breaks, many people replace the entire device, even though the fault could be repaired for a fraction of the cost. Manufacturers make it difficult by gluing components, restricting spare parts and using software that rejects replacement components. Campaigners for a "right to repair" argue that this increases waste and prevents independent shops from competing. Some governments have begun to legislate, requiring companies to supply parts and manuals for several years. Manufacturers reply that repairs by untrained people can damage batteries and create safety risks, and that tight construction makes devices thinner and more water-resistant. In the United States, some states have already passed laws forcing companies to sell parts and repair guides, and the European Union has introduced rules that require manufacturers to keep spare parts available for at least seven years. Repair cafes run by volunteers have also multiplied, and they report that most broken items brought in can be mended within an hour. Most independent repairers acknowledge these arguments but say that they could be met by training and certification, and that customers should have the choice.
quests.question: Why do manufacturers say repairs should be limited?
options: Spare parts are too cheap for repairs to be worthwhile
Phones are not designed to break in normal use
Independent shops charge too much for the work
Untrained repairs can create safety risks
quests.correctAnswer: Untrained repairs can create safety risks
quests.hint: The manufacturers' side of the argument follows "reply".
quests.explanation: They cite risks from poorly repaired batteries and the design benefits of tight construction. Campaigners answer with training and certification.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: Several countries have tested a universal basic income, a regular payment to everyone regardless of employment. In a two-year pilot, a thousand unemployed people received a monthly sum, with no conditions, while a similar group received nothing. Contrary to some predictions, recipients did not stop looking for work; on average, they were slightly more likely to find jobs, and they reported lower stress and greater trust in institutions. In a similar trial in another country, participants used the money mainly for rent and food, and only a small proportion spent it on non-essentials. Critics still worry that a permanent payment might raise prices. Governments in two other countries have announced further trials, this time with larger groups and payments that last five years. Yet the trial had limits. It lasted only two years, participants knew the payment would end, and its cost for a whole country would be enormous unless other benefits were cut. Economists therefore say that the results show only that short-term unconditional help need not discourage work, not that a permanent scheme would have the same effect.
quests.question: What do the economists conclude?
options: The trial proved that a national scheme is affordable
The results do not prove a permanent scheme would work the same way
Trust in institutions fell among the recipients
Unconditional payments discourage people from working
quests.correctAnswer: The results do not prove a permanent scheme would work the same way
quests.hint: The conclusion is in the last sentence, with "not... that" marking what they do not claim.
quests.explanation: The pilot was short and small in scope, so its results cannot simply be extended to a permanent national scheme.

quests.instruction: Read the passage efficiently, then answer the question.
quests.passage: Deep-sea mining aims to collect potato-sized nodules that lie on the ocean floor and contain metals used in batteries. Companies argue that this could reduce dependence on land mines, which cause deforestation and displace communities. Scientists, however, warn that the deep sea is poorly understood. The seabed supports slow-growing animals, some of which have been found nowhere else, and machines that scrape the bottom would create clouds of sediment. Recovery, if it occurs, could take decades or centuries. Mining companies say that the nodules are abundant and that collecting them is less destructive than digging out ore from a hillside. They also point out that the animals living there have been studied for only a few decades. Environmental groups have replied that the potential harm is too serious to risk, whatever the benefits for battery supplies. Several countries have called for a pause until more research is done, while others insist that regulation, not delay, is the answer. A study of a small test area, revisited after thirty years, found that tracks left by equipment were still visible and that few animals had returned.
quests.question: What did the revisited test area show?
options: The ecosystem had recovered fully within a few years
Animals had increased in number around the tracks
The effects of mining were still visible after thirty years
The nodules had regrown where they were removed
quests.correctAnswer: The effects of mining were still visible after thirty years
quests.hint: Look for the evidence at the end of the passage.
quests.explanation: After three decades, tracks remained and few animals had returned, supporting the concern about slow recovery.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: Smartwatches record heart rate, sleep and steps, and their makers suggest that they can warn users of health problems. Doctors acknowledge some benefits: irregular heartbeat alerts have led to diagnoses that might otherwise have been missed. But they also see downsides. Healthy people who receive false alarms may become anxious and seek unnecessary tests, which use up medical resources. In addition, the devices are less accurate for some skin tones and during vigorous movement. A study of ten thousand users found that most changed their behaviour little after buying a watch, and those who did tended to be people who were already active. Some manufacturers now market their watches directly to older customers, promising early warning of falls. A few health services have started to study whether giving watches to patients with heart conditions would reduce hospital visits. Battery life is another concern, since the more features a watch offers, the more often it needs charging, which reduces continuous monitoring. Doctors conclude that the technology helps a small group who have an actual condition, and that it should be seen as a tool for information, not a substitute for medical advice.
quests.question: According to the study, who tended to change their behaviour after buying a watch?
options: People who were already active
Doctors
Those with false alarms
People with irregular heartbeats
quests.correctAnswer: People who were already active
quests.hint: Find the study of ten thousand users.
quests.explanation: Most people changed little, and those who did were mostly already active. The heartbeat alerts are a separate benefit.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: A town in the north has created its own currency, which can be spent only in local shops. Residents can exchange regular money for the local notes at a one-to-one rate, and shops that receive them use them to pay local suppliers or staff. The idea is that money spent locally circulates several times before leaving the community, boosting trade in a way that spending in a national chain does not. The idea is not new: during the economic crisis of the 1930s, many communities used their own vouchers, and some scholars think that such schemes work best when they are tied to a shared local identity. Several banks have agreed to convert the notes back into national money at no charge, which makes shops more willing to accept them. Enthusiasts point to a rise in independent shops, while sceptics doubt the scale: the scheme's total value is small compared with the town's economy, and many businesses find it inconvenient to hold notes they cannot spend elsewhere. Even so, organisers say that the currency's greatest value is symbolic. It reminds residents that choices about where to spend have consequences for their neighbours.
quests.question: Why does the writer say the currency's value is "symbolic"?
options: Chain stores accept the notes
It makes residents aware of where their spending goes
Only symbols can be spent
The notes are worth more than ordinary money
quests.correctAnswer: It makes residents aware of where their spending goes
quests.hint: The final sentence explains the meaning of "symbolic" in plain terms.
quests.explanation: The notes highlight the effect of spending on neighbours, even if the amounts are small.

quests.instruction: Read the passage efficiently, then answer the question.
quests.passage: School meals in one country were transformed by a national programme that offered free lunches to all primary pupils. Before the change, about a third of eligible families did not claim free meals, partly from embarrassment. Once lunch was free for everyone, the stigma disappeared. The programme required schools to hire extra kitchen staff and to buy fresh ingredients from local farms, which some head teachers say improved the quality of meals. Queues at the serving counter were also shorter than before. Absence rates fell too, though the researchers say that other changes at the same time make it hard to be certain of the cause. Researchers found that pupils' concentration in afternoon lessons improved and that test scores rose slightly, especially among the lowest-income children. Parents reported saving around four hundred dollars a year per child. The cost to the government was large, but some analysts argue that it is offset by long-term benefits in health and education. Critics say that the same money might be more effectively targeted at families who need it most, but acknowledge that targeted schemes struggle to reach everyone eligible.
quests.question: Why did universal free lunches work better than targeted ones, according to the passage?
options: They were cheaper for the government than targeted ones
They were served only to children from poor families
They reduced test scores in afternoon lessons
They removed the stigma that kept families from claiming
quests.correctAnswer: They removed the stigma that kept families from claiming
quests.hint: The reason is in the sentence about a third of eligible families.
quests.explanation: Targeted schemes miss many eligible children because of embarrassment. Universal meals avoided this.

quests.instruction: Read the text and choose the best answer.
quests.passage: Rewilding is the practice of restoring land to a more natural state, often by reintroducing species that have disappeared. Advocates point to benefits beyond nature: wetlands store floodwater, and restored woodlands hold carbon. A recent project in a river valley brought back beavers, whose dams slowed the flow of water and reduced flooding in the town downstream. Ecologists in the area have recorded an increase in the number of birds and fish, and walkers now use the wetlands for recreation. Visitors have brought welcome business to a few village pubs. A local guide now leads walks in which visitors see the dams, and beavers have become something of a symbol of the valley. Farmers in the area, however, are not all enthusiastic. Some lost fields to standing water, and others worry about being told how to manage their land. Project managers have responded by offering compensation and by involving farmers in decisions. They emphasise that rewilding does not mean abandoning land, but choosing where nature can do the work at lower cost than engineering.
quests.question: How have project managers addressed farmers' concerns?
options: By removing the beavers from the valley and rebuilding drains
By buying all the farmland and turning it over to the project
By offering compensation and involving them in decisions
By abandoning the project and returning the land to farming
quests.correctAnswer: By offering compensation and involving them in decisions
quests.hint: The response is introduced by "have responded".
quests.explanation: Compensation and shared decision making are the measures mentioned. The beavers remain because they helped reduce flooding.

quests.instruction: Read the text and choose the best answer.
quests.passage: Airports are introducing facial recognition to speed up boarding. A camera matches a passenger's face with a passport photograph, and the traveller walks through without showing documents. Airlines report that the process takes seconds and reduces queues. Privacy groups, however, are uneasy. They point out that the system stores biometric information, which cannot be changed if it is stolen, unlike a password. They also question how long data is kept and whether it might be used for purposes other than boarding. Trials at several international airports have shown that the average time to board a large aircraft fell by about ten minutes, and some passengers say that they prefer not having to search for a boarding pass. Some travellers have also asked whether the cameras work reliably for people who wear head coverings or have changed appearance. Officials reply that images are deleted after the flight and that passengers may choose a manual check, though critics say that the alternative is often slower and passengers feel pressured to accept the camera. Whether the technology becomes routine may depend on whether the public trusts it.
quests.question: What is the privacy groups' particular concern about biometric data?
options: It is deleted too quickly
It takes seconds to process
It cannot be changed if stolen
It is stored on paper
quests.correctAnswer: It cannot be changed if stolen
quests.hint: Find the comparison with a password.
quests.explanation: Faces cannot be replaced like passwords, so a leak has permanent consequences. Officials say images are deleted.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: In the past, a musician needed a record label to reach a large audience. Streaming has changed this, allowing anyone to upload music, and some artists have found audiences without help from any company. However, the model rewards volume. Services pay a tiny amount per play, so an artist needs millions of plays to earn a modest income, and the algorithms that suggest songs tend to favour tracks that hook listeners in the first seconds. A few independent artists have gained a following through short clips shared on social platforms, but they usually add that turning that attention into lasting income remains difficult. Industry figures show that listeners under thirty spend more time on streaming than on any other music source. Some musicians say that this has changed how songs are written, with shorter introductions and repeated choruses. Others argue that similar pressures existed in the era of radio. A growing number of artists sell directly to fans through subscriptions, which produces less income overall but offers stability and independence.
quests.question: How has streaming influenced how songs are written, according to some musicians?
options: Songs have become longer, with slower and quieter openings
Songs have shorter introductions and repeated choruses
Songs avoid choruses to keep listeners guessing
Songs are written by record labels rather than musicians
quests.correctAnswer: Songs have shorter introductions and repeated choruses
quests.hint: The influence on song form is in the middle of the passage.
quests.explanation: Algorithms favour tracks that grab listeners quickly, prompting shorter openings. Others reply that radio also had pressures.

quests.instruction: Read the text and choose the best answer.
quests.passage: Two neighbouring towns decided to share a single fire service to save money. For the first year, the arrangement seemed a success: costs fell by fifteen percent and response times stayed the same. Then a serious fire broke out in one of the towns on the same evening that another incident occurred in the other, and the single crew had to choose. The delay in reaching the second call led to a review, in which residents were divided. The other town's mayor said that the decision to share had been taken in good faith, and that the crews had earlier helped save a neighbour's house on a night when they were stretched to the limit. Fire chiefs from both towns have promised to publish response times each quarter so that residents can judge for themselves. Some argued that the risk of simultaneous emergencies had always existed and that a shared service could not be blamed. Others said that the savings had been made by cutting staff numbers. The council has decided to keep the arrangement but to add one additional crew at peak times.
quests.question: What did the council decide after the review?
options: To end the arrangement and return to two separate services
To build a second fire station between the two towns
To reduce staff further to make larger savings
To keep the shared service and add a crew at peak times
quests.correctAnswer: To keep the shared service and add a crew at peak times
quests.hint: The decision appears in the last sentence.
quests.explanation: The service remains shared, with an extra crew at busy times. Residents disagreed about blame, but the council made a compromise.

quests.instruction: Read the passage efficiently, then answer the question.
quests.passage: A study of reading habits asked adults how many books they had read in the last year and then checked library records and purchase histories. Those who claimed to read the most were also the most likely to overstate. Nearly half of respondents said they had read more than ten books; the records supported this for barely a fifth. Researchers say that people are not lying so much as answering aspirationally, describing the reader they wish to be. The study, based on interviews with three thousand adults in five countries, also found that people were more likely to overstate when they were asked in front of someone else. Younger adults were somewhat more accurate than older ones. A follow-up survey asked the same people to keep a diary for a week, and the diaries showed a smaller but still noticeable overstatement. This matters because surveys of this kind guide policy on libraries and education. The authors suggest that questions about specific recent behaviour, such as "what did you read last week?", produce more reliable answers than general questions about the past year.
quests.question: Why does the researchers' finding matter?
options: People read fewer than ten books each year
Policy decisions often rely on survey data of this kind
Libraries have too few books for the public
Records of loans are always wrong in some way
quests.correctAnswer: Policy decisions often rely on survey data of this kind
quests.hint: Find the sentence starting "This matters because".
quests.explanation: If surveys overstate reading, policies based on them may be misguided. Specific questions improve accuracy.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: Manufacturers of plant-based milk have been growing rapidly, but the labels on their cartons have attracted controversy. Dairy producers argue that words such as "milk" and "cream" should be reserved for animal products, claiming that consumers may be confused about nutrition. Some plant-based drinks contain little protein compared with cow's milk, though others are fortified with calcium and vitamins. Regulators in several regions have ruled that the word "milk" cannot be used for products that do not come from animals, while requiring clear descriptions such as "oat drink". Producers of oat and almond drinks say that the environmental cost of their products is lower than that of dairy in terms of land and water, though nut growing needs a good deal of water in dry regions. A large study found that many consumers could not say which drinks were fortified, which suggests labels are not always read carefully. Manufacturers respond that consumers already understand the difference and that the restriction protects an industry, not shoppers. Nutritionists say that the more important issue is that people compare labels, since products vary widely.
quests.question: What do nutritionists consider the more important issue?
options: That shoppers compare the labels because products differ widely
Whether cartons are recyclable in most regions
Whether the word "milk" is allowed on a plant-based carton
Whether dairy producers are profitable enough to survive
quests.correctAnswer: That shoppers compare the labels because products differ widely
quests.hint: The nutritionists' opinion is in the last sentence.
quests.explanation: They suggest attention should go to the varying nutritional content, not to naming rules.

quests.instruction: Read the text and choose the best answer.
quests.passage: When the city introduced congestion charging, drivers entering the centre had to pay a daily fee. In the first year, traffic fell by about a fifth, journey times improved, and the revenue was invested in buses. Critics predicted that shops would lose customers, but sales in the zone rose slightly, probably because the streets became more pleasant. Some cities that studied the results have suggested that charges should vary by time of day, which would spread traffic more evenly and encourage people to use the centre outside the busiest hours. Shopkeepers, meanwhile, say that the zone has made deliveries easier for them, since vans no longer wait in long queues. After several years, however, traffic began to rise again, as more vehicles were used for deliveries and ride-hailing, which are not always charged in the same way. Officials responded by adjusting the charge for those categories and extending the hours. The lesson, they say, is that such schemes are not one-off measures but need regular adjustment, as behaviour changes.
quests.question: Why did traffic begin to rise again after several years?
options: Deliveries and ride-hailing increased and were not always charged
Shops closed and fewer people entered the charging zone
The charge was abolished after complaints from drivers
Buses were removed from the centre to make room for cars
quests.correctAnswer: Deliveries and ride-hailing increased and were not always charged
quests.hint: The reason is in the sentence beginning "After several years".
quests.explanation: Growth in vehicles not charged in the same way pushed traffic up. The officials then adjusted the scheme.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: Writers often say that the first draft is only for the writer, and that the real work is revision. Studies of professional authors suggest that this is not a comforting slogan but a description of process. Successful writers may spend more time revising than drafting, and they often set aside a draft for days to gain distance from it. In a study of student essays, those who revised after a break improved more than those who revised immediately, since the pause allowed them to see problems that had been invisible when the words were fresh. Several writers describe the discipline of returning to a text as a way of becoming a reader of one's own work. One novelist says she rewrites her opening chapter more than twenty times before she sees what the book is really about. Students who kept a log of their changes said it helped them notice patterns in their own mistakes. The authors do not claim that revision is enjoyable; many students found it tedious. They note simply that it works, and that students who understand its purpose tend to persist.
quests.question: Why did the students who took a break improve more?
options: They found the process of revision more enjoyable than writing
They wrote longer first drafts than the other students
They worked with professional authors during the break
They could see problems that were hidden when the writing was fresh
quests.correctAnswer: They could see problems that were hidden when the writing was fresh
quests.hint: The explanation follows the word "since".
quests.explanation: Distance made errors visible. The authors stress that revision is useful even if tedious.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: In a few regions, wild boar have been reappearing after centuries. Their numbers are rising because farmland has been abandoned and winters have become milder. Foresters see mixed effects: the animals dig up ground, which helps some plants, but they also damage crops, and their rooting can harm the nests of ground-nesting birds. Boar are also difficult to manage. They are intelligent, and hunting drives them into more remote areas, from where they return. Hunters report that shooting is not sufficient, as the population increases each spring, and wildlife charities have asked for fences along the busiest roads, because collisions with cars are becoming more frequent. Researchers who studied a group in the countryside noticed that families of boar move across large areas within a single night. Some towns report boar wandering at night into gardens and rubbish bins. Wildlife experts advise residents not to feed them and to secure bins, since animals that find food easily lose their fear of people and can become a danger.
quests.question: Why should residents avoid feeding boar?
options: Feeding wild animals is illegal for farmers
The animals may lose their fear of people
Foresters need boar to be hungry to control numbers
Boar cannot digest human food and become ill
quests.correctAnswer: The animals may lose their fear of people
quests.hint: The reason is at the end, following "since".
quests.explanation: Easy food makes them bold, which can be dangerous. Other options invent reasons not in the text.

quests.instruction: Read the text and choose the best answer.
quests.passage: Museums are increasingly asked whether they should charge admission. Free entry encourages more visits, especially from families and people who would not otherwise come, and in one national museum, visitor numbers rose by more than a third when charges were removed. But free entry does not guarantee a broader audience: surveys show that the additional visitors were mostly people who already came to museums and now came more often. Meanwhile, the lost income had to be replaced by government grants. In one city, the number of children who visited on school trips rose sharply once travel grants were introduced, suggesting that cost and convenience for schools can matter more than the entrance fee itself. Museum directors note that rising costs of insurance and heating make it hard to depend only on public grants. Some museums have tried compromises, such as free entry to permanent collections but a charge for special exhibitions. The evidence suggests that charging is not the only barrier to visiting; distance, time and feeling unwelcome also matter.
quests.question: What did surveys reveal about the extra visitors after charges were removed?
options: They were mainly new visitors from other regions
They were all under sixteen and came with schools
They were mostly people who already visited museums
They were tourists who came only in the summer
quests.correctAnswer: They were mostly people who already visited museums
quests.hint: The surveys are mentioned right after "But".
quests.explanation: Free entry increased repeat visits from existing museum-goers rather than broadening the audience much.

quests.instruction: Read the passage efficiently, then answer the question.
quests.passage: At a large hospital, a group of nurses noticed that patients were often woken at night for routine checks, even when they were stable. They proposed that a simple score be calculated at bedtime and that patients with low scores be left to sleep. Doctors were cautious, fearing that problems might be missed. A trial was arranged on two wards. Patients on the trial ward slept on average an hour longer, reported less confusion and were discharged half a day sooner. No cases of missed deterioration were recorded. Nurses on the trial ward were trained to use a simple chart that combines pulse, breathing rate and temperature, and they were told to call a doctor if the score rose by two points between checks. The ward's night staff reported that patients were calmer at breakfast and required fewer sleeping tablets during the trial. The hospital has extended the practice, although it still uses the old routine for patients recovering from major surgery, in whom rapid changes are more likely. The nurses say the change shows the value of asking why a routine exists.
quests.question: Why does the hospital still use the old routine for some patients?
options: Patients demanded frequent checks after every operation
Rapid changes are more likely after major surgery
Doctors refused to accept the new routine at all
The trial showed poor results on the trial ward
quests.correctAnswer: Rapid changes are more likely after major surgery
quests.hint: Find the exception at the end of the passage.
quests.explanation: For patients recovering from major surgery, deterioration can occur quickly, so frequent checks remain.

quests.instruction: Read the passage efficiently, then answer the question.
quests.passage: The claim that people use only ten percent of their brains is widely repeated but false. Brain scans show that virtually all regions are active over the course of a day, and even during sleep, many areas remain busy. Damage to almost any part of the brain has effects, which would not happen if most of it were idle. The myth may have originated in early studies that overlooked the functions of large areas, or in motivational writing that promised hidden potential. Its persistence tells us something: people like the idea that an untapped reserve lies within them. Some researchers think the number may come from an old remark by a psychologist, who suggested that people rarely use their full potential, which later writers turned into a claim about physical brain tissue. Brain imaging has also shown that people who learn a new skill, such as juggling, develop measurable changes in connected areas within weeks. Neuroscientists suggest that a more accurate and equally encouraging message is that the brain can change with practice, forming new connections throughout life.
quests.question: What alternative message do neuroscientists suggest?
options: Brain damage rarely matters in adults
People use all of their brain at exactly the same time
The brain can change with practice throughout life
Most brain areas are unused in daily life
quests.correctAnswer: The brain can change with practice throughout life
quests.hint: The alternative is at the end, introduced by "more accurate".
quests.explanation: Instead of a hidden reserve, they emphasise that the brain builds new connections with practice.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: Companies that ask staff to return to the office often cite creativity and collaboration. Employees reply that they can concentrate better at home and resent the commute. A study of a large firm that required three days a week in the office found that senior staff, who supported the policy, and junior staff, who were less enthusiastic, both reported benefits: juniors learned faster when they sat near experienced colleagues, and seniors valued informal contact. However, the policy also led to greater resignation among the most experienced workers, who had the easiest time finding jobs elsewhere. Some of the firm's managers argue that the departures were caused by the timing of the announcement, made just before a wave of hiring in the industry, rather than by the policy itself. The company has since introduced a rota that lets teams decide on their own office days, and early figures show fewer resignations. The researchers suggest that flexibility itself may be a valued benefit and that companies which remove it must offer something in return. They do not claim that remote work is better, only that people react to lost freedom.
quests.question: What effect on experienced workers did the policy have?
options: They preferred the commute
They worked from home more
More of them resigned
They learned faster
quests.correctAnswer: More of them resigned
quests.hint: The negative effect follows "However".
quests.explanation: The most experienced workers could easily find other jobs, so more left. Juniors gained from proximity.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: A famous psychology experiment suggested that people who were told to hold a pen in their teeth, forcing a smile, found cartoons funnier than those who held it with their lips. The result was cited in textbooks for decades. Then, several laboratories attempted to reproduce it. Their combined results showed no effect. The original authors argued that the replications differed in details, such as the presence of a camera that made participants self-conscious. The dispute has become a case study of scientific practice. One critic has observed that the failure to reproduce results in psychology is not unique to that field, and that medicine and economics face similar problems when studies are small or when researchers have many choices about how to analyse data. Some journals now publish studies before results are known, on the condition that the method is sound, so that null findings are not hidden. Rather than proving that the original finding was false, the outcome shows that a single study cannot settle a question. Researchers now more often publish plans in advance and share data so that others can check how results were reached.
quests.question: What does the case show about science?
options: A single study cannot settle a question
Smiling has no effect on mood
Cameras invalidate experiments
Psychology experiments are always false
quests.correctAnswer: A single study cannot settle a question
quests.hint: The lesson is in the sentence beginning "Rather than".
quests.explanation: The outcome demonstrates the need for replication, not that the first result was necessarily false.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: A coastal city has decided to move its main port ten kilometres along the shore, freeing waterfront land for housing. Supporters say the move will allow larger ships to dock and will transform the waterfront. Yet the port employs six thousand people, and workers fear that jobs will be lost during the transition. The plan includes a fund for retraining, but unions say that experienced crane operators cannot easily be retrained as office staff. The port authority expects to lease a third of the vacated land to developers and to keep the remainder as open space, including a wide promenade that will be open to the public throughout the year. A short ferry service is planned to link the old port area with the new one, to keep the harbour history visible. Local shopkeepers, on the other hand, expect more customers as residents arrive. A study by the city suggests that the net effect on employment will be positive after ten years but negative in the first three, a pattern that critics say is easy to forget when the benefits lie so far in the future.
quests.question: What is the pattern that critics say is easy to forget?
options: Housing is built before the port is moved
Shops lose customers during the first years
Job losses come first and benefits arrive later
Retraining is never funded by the city
quests.correctAnswer: Job losses come first and benefits arrive later
quests.hint: The pattern is described at the end.
quests.explanation: The city's own study shows negative effects in the first three years and gains later, which critics say leaders may overlook.

quests.instruction: Read the passage efficiently, then answer the question.
quests.passage: Some restaurants have removed prices from menus for customers who are guests of someone else, so that the host alone sees the cost. The practice is meant to spare guests embarrassment and to allow them to choose freely. Studies show that in such cases people tend to order more expensive dishes, which suits the restaurant. Other restaurants have replaced tipping with a service charge included in the price, arguing that it is fairer to kitchen staff, who rarely share in tips. A famous chain in one city tried adding a small charge to bookings that were not honoured, and found that no-shows dropped by nearly half, though it also received several complaints from customers who felt they were being penalised. Owners of small cafes added that removing prices from some menus made customers less nervous about asking for extras. Customers' reactions are mixed: some feel that the price is less honest, while others like knowing the total cost. In each case, the design of a bill, the researchers say, influences behaviour in ways that customers seldom notice.
quests.question: What is the researchers' overall point?
options: Guests always choose the cheapest dishes on offer
Tipping is unfair to customers who pay by card
Restaurants should abolish menus and printed bills
The way a bill is designed influences behaviour unnoticed
quests.correctAnswer: The way a bill is designed influences behaviour unnoticed
quests.hint: The overall point is in the last sentence, generalising from the examples.
quests.explanation: Both examples show how presentation of costs affects choices. The final sentence states the general message.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: Climate scientists often describe "tipping points", thresholds beyond which a system changes abruptly and cannot easily return. The melting of ice sheets or the drying of a rainforest are examples. The concept is powerful but also open to misunderstanding. Some people conclude that nothing matters until a threshold is crossed, while others assume that once one is passed, the situation is hopeless. Researchers stress that neither is correct. The risk of crossing a threshold increases gradually with warming, so every fraction of a degree changes the odds. And even after a threshold is crossed, the consequences depend on speed and scale, which human actions can still influence. A recent review of past climate records suggests that some systems, such as monsoon patterns, have shifted rapidly in the past, which makes the concept more than theoretical. Nevertheless, many thresholds are still poorly understood. Some economists compare the idea to a slope that becomes steeper: the further one goes, the harder it becomes to stop. The concept, they say, should motivate action, not paralysis.
quests.question: What do researchers say about crossing a threshold?
options: It is impossible to predict when it will happen
It happens suddenly with no warning of any kind
Nothing can then be done to change the outcome
Its consequences can still be influenced by human action
quests.correctAnswer: Its consequences can still be influenced by human action
quests.hint: The researchers reject two opposite conclusions; find their positive point.
quests.explanation: They stress that speed and scale of consequences remain open to influence, so action still matters.

quests.instruction: Read the passage efficiently, then answer the question.
quests.passage: A small publisher decided to release a novel in weekly instalments by email, as newspapers did in the nineteenth century. Subscribers received a chapter every Friday and could reply to the author. The experiment attracted three thousand readers, many of whom said that the pace suited them; they read a chapter slowly, discussed it with friends and remembered the plot better than they would have with a book. Some, however, found it frustrating to wait, and about a fifth stopped before the end. The author's mailbox filled with suggestions, including a letter from a reader in another country who wanted a character to be given a happier ending. She replied to every message within a week. The publisher noticed that open rates for emails were highest on Friday mornings and lowest on Sunday evenings. The author says that the reactions influenced later chapters, since a subplot that readers disliked was shortened. The publisher plans a second series, and considers that the format may suit novels with strong endings to each episode.
quests.question: How did readers' reactions affect the novel?
options: The ending was changed
A disliked subplot was shortened
The novel was published as a book
Subscribers wrote chapters
quests.correctAnswer: A disliked subplot was shortened
quests.hint: The effect is stated in the sentence containing "since".
quests.explanation: The author responded to feedback by reducing a subplot readers disliked. The ending is not said to change.

quests.instruction: Read the text and choose the best answer.
quests.passage: The city has decided to close a small hospital and replace it with a larger one further away. Planners argue that patients will receive better care, since specialised equipment and experts can be concentrated in one place, and the evidence for stroke and heart attack is convincing. However, journey times will be longer for some villagers, and the sums used for calculations assume that ambulances travel at average speeds on roads that are often blocked in winter. In a comparable case abroad, the new hospital took two years longer than planned to complete, and during that time patients travelled even farther. The local newspaper has begun to track ambulance arrival times. The health authority says that helicopters can reach the remote villages but only in good weather, which is not guaranteed in winter. Residents point out that a fast ambulance is meaningless if the road is closed. The health authority has promised a study of winter access, but has not delayed the decision. Whether patients benefit will depend on details that are easier to specify on paper than to guarantee on a snowy road.
quests.question: What is the residents' objection?
options: Calculations ignore winter road conditions
Specialised equipment is unnecessary
Ambulances are too fast
The new hospital is too small
quests.correctAnswer: Calculations ignore winter road conditions
quests.hint: The residents' objection follows the mention of average speeds.
quests.explanation: The planners' figures assume normal speeds, but winter closures could make journeys longer.
